Imagine waking up one morning and finding that everything you know—your home, your neighborhood, even the trust in your country—has suddenly changed. Fear and suspicion are sweeping across the nation, and for one Japanese American family, life is about to turn upside down. Welcome to a journey that invites us to walk in the shoes of Jeanne Wakatsuki Houston, as she shares her family’s true story in Farewell to Manzanar: A True Story of Japanese American Experience During and After the World War II Internment. We’ll explore what it means to be uprooted—forced from your home and thrust behind barbed wire, all because of war and prejudice. But this isn’t just a lesson in history; it’s about identity, resilience, and the ache of loss. We’ll feel the quiet strength it takes to hold on to dignity, the way family bonds can shift under pressure, and how the search for belonging can sometimes feel out of reach in a country that suddenly feels unfamiliar.
As we move through the daily rhythms of camp life, you’ll notice the small acts of endurance—and the cracks that begin to show when people are pushed to their limits. And when the gates finally open, the journey doesn’t end. The challenge of rebuilding, of finding your place again in a changed America, brings a whole new set of questions. Together, we’ll uncover how prejudice lingers, how cultural identity becomes both shield and struggle, and where hope for acceptance and understanding can be found—sometimes in the most unexpected places. Through personal memory, Jeanne’s story opens a window into what home and family truly mean—and why the quest for justice is never just about the past. So, are you ready to step inside this powerful story, and discover what echoes beyond the fences of Manzanar?
